text: You have houses laid out as a binary tree. Each node holds an amount of money. You can't rob two houses that are directly linked — so never a parent and its own child. Return the most money you can rob.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the only rule is that a parent and its child can't both be robbed. A grandparent and a grandchild are fine, because they are not directly linked. Is that right?
That's right.

Then I already see the shape. Every node has two choices: rob it, or skip it. If I rob it, both children are off limits, so the rest comes from the four grandchildren. If I skip it, both children are free. A node's answer only depends on its own subtree, so I can solve it bottom up.
Are there any constraints on the input size? And can a node's value be zero?
Up to ten to the fourth nodes. Each value is between zero and ten to the fourth. So yes, zero is a legal value.

Good, I'll keep the zero in mind. Overflow first: ten thousand nodes all worth ten thousand, on a perfect tree, give about sixty-six point six five million — three point one percent of the int maximum. So plain int is safe. Also, a chain can be ten thousand deep; I'll come back to the stack.

Let me run through the example: three, two, three, null, three, null, one. The root's children are two and three, each with one right child, three and one. Robbing the root gives three plus three plus one, seven. Skipping it gives the best of each child, three plus three, six. So seven. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would try every valid set of houses — exponentially many, so at ten to the fourth nodes it never finishes. This problem reminds me of dynamic programming on a tree: a take-it-or-skip-it choice per node, where the state is a subtree. The recursion alone is still exponential, because both branches reach into the same grandchildren. So I'll add a memo keyed by node pointer. Each node is solved once, and the whole thing becomes linear time.

Here's the plan. One: rob of null is zero. Two: rob this is the node's value plus its four grandchildren; skip this is rob of left plus rob of right. Three: take the max and cache it by node pointer. One thing worth flagging — the key must be the pointer, not the value, since two nodes can share a value over different subtrees. There's a trade-off here: a post-order pass returning a rob and skip pair needs no map at all. I'm picking the memo because the rob-or-skip story reads directly off the code, and the time is the same. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code it up.

Alright, let me code this up. The memo is a class member. Null returns zero, and a cached node returns its answer. Then I collect the four grandchildren, and return the max of rob this and skip this, storing it in the memo on the same line. One thing worth flagging — the if-left and if-right guards exist so I can write left's left without dereferencing a null pointer. When a child is missing, its two values stay at zero, which is exactly what a missing subtree is worth.

Let's dry-run the code on the example, expecting seven. Call the root A, its children B and C, then D under B and E under C. The row that matters is rob of B: D was already solved as A's grandchild, so when the skip branch asks again, it comes straight out of the map. That overlap is what would blow up without a cache. A is seven against six, so seven. That matches. The whole run is nineteen calls: five first-time nodes, two repeats, and twelve on null.

Let's also test with corner cases. An empty tree returns zero from the first line. A single node returns its own value, since skip this is zero. And the second example, three, four, five, one, three, null, one, gives nine — skip the root, take four and five.
The answers look right. You flagged earlier that a node's value can be zero. What happens to this code then?

Let me think about that. Good question — that's the line I marked, and my cache check is wrong. It tests the value, not whether the key is there. A subtree whose true answer is zero stores zero, which reads back as false, so that node is recomputed every single time. The answers stay correct; this is purely a speed bug. And the bracket lookup on a miss inserts a zero entry, so the map still ends at exactly the node count. That's why it's easy to miss.
How bad does it get?

With the memo dead, a long chain is exactly un-memoized Fibonacci. On an all-zero chain, every added node multiplies the calls by one point six one eight, the golden ratio. Forty nodes already take eight hundred sixty-seven million calls and three point two seven seconds, so about forty-five nodes times out — far under the limit. And it really is the zeros: the same chain with values of one makes just a hundred nineteen calls at thirty nodes.
Would a big all-zero tree always be that bad?

No, and that's the interesting part. The real discriminator is depth, not the zeros alone. Zeros kill the memo; depth turns that into an exponential. A perfect all-zero tree is only log n deep, so calls grow roughly n to the one point six nine. At ten thousand nodes it finishes in about thirty-five milliseconds — about fifty times slower than it should be, but it passes. Only the deep chain actually dies.
So how do you fix it?

It's one word. Ask whether the key is present, with memo dot count, instead of whether the value is truthy. The fix gives identical answers on over a million test cases — purely a performance fix. With it, the call count is exactly four n minus one for any tree shape. That's clean linear time.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear with a working memo — each node is solved once, with a fixed amount of work. Space is the tree height for the stack plus linear for the map. In the worst case the tree is a single chain. Measured without optimization, a frame is about fifty-six bytes, and the default eight megabyte stack survives about a hundred forty-nine thousand levels, so ten to the fourth has a fourteen point nine four times margin. This isn't a tail call, so the compiler can't flatten it.

Oh, one more thing — the map is a class member on the heap, so it costs nothing per recursive call. If I wanted only height-sized space, I'd switch to the pair version: one post-order pass returning rob and skip, and no map at all. Same time, less space.
Last one — what are the common ways people get this wrong?

Four I'd watch for. Adding the node's value to both branches — caught by one, one. Summing even levels against odd levels — zero, zero, one, one gives one when the answer is two. Keying the memo on the value — zero, zero, zero, one breaks it. And dropping a grandchild term, caught by one, null, zero, null, one.

Three things stood out. You named the rob-or-skip structure before writing a line. You found a real bug in your own cache check from one constraint, and you were precise that it costs speed, not correctness. And you separated the zeros from the depth — the chain hits the golden ratio while the perfect tree still passes — then fixed it with one word. That's a strong hire.
